request.query: AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML price increase October 7 2026

results.title: AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks Price Hike: One of Four Rises
results.author: Sofia Lindström
highlights:
AWS raised the hourly rates of EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML by roughly 20% in July 2026, across six instance families (P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en and P4de), and the fourth rise of the year followed: on October 7, 2026 AWS raised the rates again, by 15% on most families, so that on eCorpIT’s page, read on November 2, 2026, P6-B300 bills at $16.146 per accelerator-hour outside GovCloud, up from $14.04 in July. The scope is Capacity Blocks, which AWS’s EC2 pricing page describes as a way to reserve GPU instances in advance for ML workloads. The July start date is reported two ways: AWS notified customers on June 26 of a July 1 start (TECHi), while eCorpIT says AWS’s own revised notice moved it to July 7. eCorpIT reports that AWS says the next update is due in January 2027.

## Four rises in 2026, and where July’s 20% falls

According to eCorpIT, AWS made the July change on its pricing page without a blog post or customer advisory: the notice and the new rates appeared on the Capacity Blocks pricing page, and the October rise took the same route. AWS’s pricing page is therefore where a change shows up. The four steps eCorpIT lists, plus the date AWS has given for the next update:

| Date | What changed | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| January 3 | H200-linked rates up 15%: p5e.48xlarge from $34.61 to $39.80 an hour in most regions, and from $43.26 to $49.75 in US West (N. California) | eCorpIT |
| April 1 | 10% rise on US P5, P5en and P6-B200 rates | eCorpIT |
| July | About 20% on six families; effective July 1 per the June 26 notice, July 7 per AWS’s revised notice | TECHi, eCorpIT |
| October 7 | 15% on most families, about 26.5% on P5 and P5en outside the US | eCorpIT |
| January 2027 | Next update due, as AWS states it | eCorpIT |

The steps compound, so the total is larger than any single headline. TECHi puts January plus July at roughly 38% since December. VentureBeat counts four AWS Capacity Block increases in 2026. October lifts the total further, as the single-instance series below shows.

## Family by family: the October 7 rates

The table lists the October 7 rate per accelerator-hour for each family, as eCorpIT reports the schedule. eCorpIT’s page, read on November 2, 2026, says AWS now lists one Capacity Block rate across regions, apart from GovCloud on P6, and puts P5 at $5.970 per accelerator-hour in all listed regions. AWS’s own Capacity Blocks pricing page also lists P4d, which is not among the six July families, at $1.696 per accelerator-hour for standard AWS regions, the cheapest Nvidia family on that schedule.

| Family | October 7 rate per accelerator-hour | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| P6-B300 | $16.146 | Outside GovCloud; up 15% from $14.04 in July |
| P6-B200 | $14.208 | Outside GovCloud; up 15% from $12.355 in July |
| P5 | $5.970 | All listed regions, per eCorpIT; up 15% from $5.191 in US regions and about 26.5% from $4.72 outside the US, July rates |
| P5e | $6.866 | Up 15% from $5.97 in July; used in the p5e.48xlarge series below |
| P5en | $7.895 | Outside GovCloud; up 15% from $6.865 in US regions and about 26.5% from $6.241 elsewhere, July rates |
| P4de | $2.546 | Outside GovCloud; up 15% from $2.214 in US regions in July |
| P4d | $1.696 | Standard AWS regions, from AWS’s Capacity Blocks pricing page |

eCorpIT puts the October rise at 15% on most families, and P6-B300 shows it: $14.04 to $16.146 is 15%. P5 and P5en outside the US are the exception, at about 26.5%. That larger figure sits next to a change in how rates are listed, since eCorpIT’s page says AWS now lists one rate across regions, apart from GovCloud on P6.

Eight accelerators make an instance, so p5.48xlarge now costs $47.76 an hour ($5.970 times eight), and eCorpIT’s own figure for an eight-GPU B300 block at $16.146 is about $129 an hour. Tracing one instance through the steps shows the cumulative effect. The p5e.48xlarge cost $34.61 an hour before January 3 and $39.80 after it, per eCorpIT. Taking eight accelerators per instance, October’s $6.866 makes it $54.93 an hour, which is 58.7% above where the year began and well past the 38% TECHi counted after July.

## What one block costs once the OS fee and the upfront charge are in

A Capacity Block runs for 1 to 14 days or a multiple of 7 days up to 182 days, with up to 64 instances per block (512 GPUs at eight per instance), and it can be scheduled up to 8 weeks ahead, according to AWS’s Capacity Blocks documentation. AWS’s billing documentation says the block price is charged up front, with the payment landing on your account between 5 minutes and 12 hours after purchase. From the start of the block, the running charge is the operating system fee alone.

The OS charge is a separate line item. In AWS’s worked example, a reservation price of $31.464 per instance-hour produced a $6,041.088 reservation charge, and an operating-system price of $1.8432 per instance-hour produced a further $346.52. A budget built from the reservation rate alone comes up short, and the cash for the first line leaves the account within hours of booking.

For scale, eCorpIT prices one 8-GPU B300 block at about $129 an hour, roughly $43,400 for two weeks, before storage, networking and egress. TECHi priced eight P6-B300 nodes (64 accelerators) for 30 days at about $647,000 at July’s $14.04, against roughly $539,000 before July. A 30-day block is not a bookable length, so we repriced the same cluster for 28 days, or 672 hours, which is 43,008 accelerator-hours. TECHi’s $539,000 over 46,080 accelerator-hours implies about $11.70 an hour before July. At that rate 28 days costs about $503,000, at July’s $14.04 about $604,000, and at October’s $16.146 about $694,000. The same cluster for the same length now costs about $191,000 more than it did before July, before any OS fee.

## Quinn and Jain disagree on why AWS keeps raising Capacity Block rates

AWS’s stated reason, as eCorpIT quotes it, is that Capacity Block pricing varies with supply and demand and that the adjustment “reflects the supply/demand patterns we expect this quarter.” Two outside voices split on that. Cloud economist Corey Quinn calls the change “a policy decision, not supply/demand”, on the grounds that AWS updated published base rates. Analyst Pareekh Jain says the “most defensible explanation is simply market-based pricing tied to supply and demand.”

The cadence leans toward Quinn’s reading, though it does not settle the question. Four rises in 2026 landed on January 3, April 1, July and October 7, each upward, and AWS has already named January 2027 for the next update. A list-price schedule reviewed each quarter can be announced ahead of time, and AWS’s own phrase “this quarter” fits that reading. Demand is still real, since Jain’s explanation and a schedule can both be true at once, and nothing in the sources rules out another step. January looks like a scheduled review that has gone up every time so far.

...

Rank.ai’s November 10, 2026 snapshot lists on-demand p5.48xlarge at $55.04 an hour in us-east-1, or $6.88 per GPU-hour. A Capacity Block at the October 7 P5 rate of $5.970 per accelerator-hour is $47.76 an hour, 13% below that list price. On-demand P5 pricing was also cut earlier: as of November 13, 2026, AWS’s June 5, 2025 announcement says the P5 reduction of up to 45% applied to On-Demand pricing from June 1, 2025 and to Savings Plan purchases after June 4, 2025.

...

Convergedigest reports that customers pay the prevailing rate when the reservation is purchased, even if the reserved capacity starts after a future price change. AWS’s billing documentation agrees on the mechanics: a search across a range of dates returns the lowest-priced offering available, and once you have reserved a block its price does not change. With blocks bookable up to 8 weeks ahead, a block bought before the January 2027 update can start weeks later at the old rate. AWS gives only “January 2027” for that update, and the first 2026 rise landed on January 3, so do not assume you have the whole month. VentureBeat’s advice is to check Capacity Block rates before buying, since AWS has raised them four times in 2026.

results.title: GPU Rental Prices Are Rising Again: What the October 2026 Nebius and AWS Changes Mean for Inference Cost
highlights:
After falling in 2025, H100 rental prices rose in 2026. Nebius raised list prices on 1 October and AWS raised Capacity Blocks on 7 October. Here is what the numbers show and how to plan for them.

...

In short

- GPU rental prices fell in 2025 and are rising in 2026. Nebius raised its H100 on-demand price from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU-hour on 1 October 2026.
- AWS raised EC2 Capacity Blocks prices by about 15% in October. AWS on-demand prices did not change.
- One price index put the median on-demand H100 SXM at $4.20 per GPU-hour on 7 October 2026. Hyperscalers charged a median of $10.53 for the same GPU.
- The "price per GPU-hour" you see is a list price. Your real cost per token depends on utilization, and a half-idle GPU costs twice as much per token.
- Plan for price drift: use commitments for steady load, keep workloads portable, and track cost per token, not cost per hour.

...

## What changed in October 2026

Key point

Two large providers raised GPU prices within a week of each other, reversing the 2025 trend.

The Uvik GPU Price Index (captured 7 October 2026) lists the dated events. On 1 October, Nebius raised H100 on-demand from $3.85 to $4.50 (+17%). It raised H200 from $4.50 to $5.40 (+20%). On 7 October, AWS raised EC2 Capacity Blocks prices by about 15%.

The Nebius pricing page I fetched today matches the new numbers. It lists H100 at $4.50, H200 at $5.40, B200 at $8.50 and B300 at $9.50 per GPU-hour. It also says prices may change at any time.

IntuitionLabs checked AWS on 10 October 2026. The Capacity Blocks rate for P5 (H100) is $5.970 per GPU. In July 2026 it was $5.191 in US regions and $4.720 in other regions. By my calculation from those figures, that is about +15% in the US and about +26.5% elsewhere. AWS says the rates are next scheduled to be updated in January 2027.

Note

Capacity Blocks are reservations, not on-demand. IntuitionLabs warns against using them for cross-provider comparison. AWS on-demand prices did not change in this round.

...

- After falling in 2025, GPU rental prices rose in 2026: on 1 October 2026 Nebius raised H100 on-demand from $3.85 to $4.50 (+17%) and H200 ... $4.50 to $5.40; AWS raised EC2 Capacity Blocks by about 15% (a reservation product, not on-demand, which did not change; next update scheduled January 2027).
- The Uvik index (19 providers, 87 public on-demand prices) put the median H100 SXM at $4.20 per GPU-hour on 7 October, with a hyperscaler median of $10.53 versus $3.95 for 12 GPU clouds (2.7x). Three-year commitments cut H100 prices by 56% to 57% at the big three.
- Which provider you rent from matters more than the month you rent in.

results.title: The bill is increasing even though prices haven't been raised | What is actually happening with AWS, Azure, and GCP｜梟 〜GLEANINGS〜
results.author: 梟 〜GLEANINGS〜
highlights:
This is a sentence that always comes up when talking about cloud costs since the beginning of 2026. And it is half true. As of September 2026, there has been no official announcement that the three companies have collectively raised the base prices for general-purpose compute or storage.

...

### There is certainly no sign of a blanket increase in base prices

I checked the AWS pricing page and What's New, Microsoft's licensing notices and Partner Center announcements, and the Google Cloud pricing change notification page. I went through them all, and as of September 2, 2026, there is no official announcement that base prices for general-purpose compute and storage are being raised across the board.

In response to an inquiry from DatacenterDynamics, AWS replied, “AWS's commitment to not raise pricing on fixed pricing models like On Demand and Savings Plans remains unchanged.” This is a statement that their policy of not raising prices for fixed-price models like On Demand and Savings Plans remains unchanged. The price revisions Microsoft made in 2026 were for Microsoft 365 (SaaS), which is a separate matter from the Azure infrastructure. What is listed on the Google Cloud “Infrastructure Services and Pricing Updates” page is still the content of the revisions implemented in October 2022 and April 2023.

...

### AWS GPU reservation slots have already gone up twice

However, it is not the case that there are no price increases at all.

AWS has a menu called EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML, which allows you to reserve GPU computing resources for a set period. This pricing page states the following:

“Reservation prices are updated regularly based on trends in supply and demand for EC2 Capacity Blocks. The current prices are scheduled to be updated next in October, 2026.”

They are updated regularly based on supply and demand, with the next revision scheduled for October 2026. In other words, this menu is designed with the premise that prices will fluctuate.

In fact, it has moved twice since the beginning of 2026. In January, the p5e.48xlarge equipped with NVIDIA H200 was revised from $34.61 to $39.80 per hour in most regions, and the p5en.48xlarge was revised from $36.18 to $41.61. In July, after initially being announced for July 1 and then changed to July 7, the revisions covered P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en, and P4de. The P6-B300 is at a level of $14.04 per hour per accelerator.

The prices for January mentioned here are only the amounts after the revision as of January. Because it went up again in July, the p5e.48xlarge currently on the pricing page is $47.76 per hour. That is exactly a 20 percent increase from $39.80.

AWS does not publish these revision rates. Since they do not keep old prices, the figures of “15 percent” and “20 percent” are calculated by news organizations and technical blogs that kept records of the price lists before and after the revisions. They are simply separate calculation results lined up, such as the January revision being exactly 15 percent and the July P5 revision being exactly 20 percent. It is not that AWS said “we are raising prices by 15 to 20 percent,” and the new and old prices themselves mentioned above are also based on the records of the reporting side.

And one more point. There are no individual notifications for these revisions in AWS's What's New or on their blog. What exists is the fact that the pricing page has been rewritten and the next scheduled update notice appearing in small print on that page. Price increases are being carried out in a way that you cannot notice unless you go looking for them.

...

- As of September 2026, there has been no official announcement that AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud have generally raised base prices for general-purpose compute and storage.
- However, prices have risen in specific areas. AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML were revised twice, in January and July 2026, and the pricing page states that the next revision is scheduled for October 2026. AWS has not disclosed the revision rate, and the "15 to 20 percent" figure circulating is a value back-calculated from the old and new prices.
- Google Cloud raised prices for egress via CDN Interconnect, Direct Peering, and Carrier Peering starting May 1, 2026. In North America, the price doubled from $0.04 to $0.08 per GiB. Cloud CDN itself and general egress are not affected.
- For all three companies, the structure in Japan is that list prices are in dollars, while billing is in yen. Azure determines the rate based on the London closing price two business days before the end of the previous month, Google Cloud at the beginning of each month, and AWS at the time the invoice is created. The Japanese yen is not included in Google Cloud's currency fluctuation protection target currencies.
- Therefore, even if the provider does not raise prices, the billed amount will increase if the yen weakens. The standard foreign exchange rate has gone from 145 yen in July 2025 to 163 yen for the September 2026 application period.
- Domestically, Fujitsu will implement price revisions for FJcloud-V and others on October 1, 2026. The revision rates have not been publicly disclosed to that extent.
- In the State of FinOps 2026, 98 percent of organizations responded that they are managing AI spending (up from 31 percent two years ago), and SaaS spending management has reached 90 percent.

results.title: AWS raises GPU prices 20% as the memory crunch bites
results.author: Darius Popa
highlights: Amazon Web Services has raised prices for EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML by roughly 20%, starting in July. Business Insider first reported the change, and AWS confirmed it. The service lets companies reserve Nvidia GPUs in advance, so a long training run keeps going instead of stalling halfway.

results.title: AWS Raises GPU Instance Prices Twice in 2026, Breaking Its Own Pattern | TechShorts Blog
results.author: Bhavika J
highlights:
AWS raised prices on EC2 Capacity Blocks, the reservation model customers use to guarantee GPU capacity for short, fixed windows, on January 4, 2026 and again on July 1, 2026. The two increases compound to roughly 38 percent on the instance types most affected, including the p5e.48xlarge family (Network World, 2026; DataCenterDynamics, 2026).

Under AWS's current published rates, Capacity Blocks for ML now run $14.04 per accelerator-hour for P6-B300 instances, $12.355 for P6-B200, and $5.191 for P5, with older P4de capacity at $2.214 (Network World, 2026). AWS attributed the change to supply and demand for GPU capacity rather than any change in the underlying hardware cost, according to comments the company gave reporters (IT Pro, 2026).

results.title: AWS Raised GPU Prices Twice in Six Months: What It Signals and What to Do About It - Data Storage
results.author: DataStorage Editorial Team
highlights:
An AWS p5e.48xlarge Capacity Block reservation, eight NVIDIA H200 GPUs bundled into a single instance, cost $34.61 an hour in December 2025. AWS raised that rate to $39.80 on January 4, 2026, a quiet, weekend announcement with no advance customer notice. Then, on July 1, 2026, AWS raised it again, this time to roughly $47.76 an hour. That's a 38 percent cumulative increase in six months, on a product enterprises specifically pay a premium for because it guarantees GPU capacity will be there when a training run needs to start.

...

| Metric | January 4, 2026 | July 1, 2026 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Increase | ~15% | ~20% |
| Families affected | P5e, P5en (H200-based) | P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en, P4de |
| Example: p5e.48xlarge | $34.61 to $39.80/hr | $39.80 to ~$47.76/hr |
| Advance notice | None, posted over a weekend | Published on AWS documentation page |

The January hike affected P5e and P5en instances specifically, the H200-based families. The July hike was broader, covering P6-B300 and P6-B200 (AWS's Blackwell-generation instances), plus P5, P5e, P5en, and P4de, essentially AWS's entire GPU reservation lineup. Older instance families saw smaller dollar increases but similar percentage jumps, meaning this wasn't a single product line getting repriced, it was the whole Capacity Blocks catalog.

...

Capacity Blocks for ML are AWS's reserve-ahead product: you commit to a fixed block of GPU accelerators for a defined future time window and pay upfront for the guarantee that hardware will be available when your window starts. This is what got the two hikes covered here.

results.title: Medium
results.author: allglenn
highlights: On June 26, 2026, AWS updated its published Capacity Blocks pricing page with new per-accelerator hourly rates effective July 1, roughly a 20% increase across every major instance family. Reporting that cross-referenced AWS’s own documentation puts the new US-region rates at: the P6-B300 billed at $14.04, the P6-B200 at $12.355, the P5 (US regions) at $5.191, the P5 (non-US) at $4.72, the P5e at $5.97, the P5en (US) at $6.865, the P5en (non-US) at $6.241, and the P4de (US) at $2.214 per accelerator-hour. AWS’s stated rationale, repeated verbatim from the January adjustment, is that “EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML pricing vary based on supply and demand patterns… This price adjustment reflects the supply/demand patterns we expect this quarter.”

results.title: EU Sovereign Cloud Providers Pay Spot Prices on Chips
results.author: Andrei Nutas
highlights: For comparison, Amazon buys DRAM and NAND in the same overheated market. Yet so far its prices have barely moved. It has raised EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML, one reserved GPU product, by about 20 percent from July on top of roughly 15 percent in January, and left everything else untouched, including instances running Trainium, the accelerator it designs itself. This was also done without an announcement. The new numbers appeared on the pricing page, and after Business Insider reported them AWS said only that Capacity Blocks prices “are updated periodically based on supply and demand.”
